items.title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
authors: Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin
items.preview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.

reading.overview: A kill switch to shut down dangerous AI systems is a seductive concept, but the metaphor hides how the models work – and how they get out of control in the first place.
reading.notice: This is a short description supplied by the publisher feed, not a full-article review or independent assessment.

digest.idea: A single kill switch cannot stand in for continuous oversight of distributed AI systems and human decisions.
digest.explain: The idea of a single emergency switch makes AI governance look like a matter of one decisive act. Wintermeier argues that this image hides the distributed infrastructure of advanced systems and the human decisions that shape their behavior before any emergency occurs.
digest.interpretation: For agents that organize attention or act on a user's behalf, a clear stop or revoke button is necessary but not sufficient. Designers should also disclose whose instructions an agent follows, what permissions it holds, how people can review earlier actions, and which dependencies may keep working after an interaction is stopped. These are applications of Wintermeier's reasoning to attention technologies, not outcomes demonstrated by this article.
digest.limitation: This is a rhetoric- and governance-centered expert commentary, not an empirical evaluation of frontier AI controls. It describes particular incidents and policy proposals from 2026; those circumstances are context for the author's argument, not a systematic sample of AI failures.

longform.thesis: The idea of a single emergency switch makes AI governance look like a matter of one decisive act. Wintermeier argues that this image hides the distributed infrastructure of advanced systems and the human decisions that shape their behavior before any emergency occurs.
longform.reasoning: The essay treats a kill switch as a political and technological metaphor rather than only a device specification. A switch implies a bounded machine, an identifiable point of control and an operator who can intervene once a problem is visible. That mental picture is a poor fit for advanced AI deployed across interconnected services, data centers, models and users. Even if a particular model can be disabled, the metaphor does not specify who could halt associated processes or what would remain active elsewhere. Wintermeier connects this limitation to the familiar image of AI as a black box. Both metaphors encourage readers to imagine a single opaque object, instead of asking how infrastructures, organizations and choices interact. Crucially, the metaphor also places people outside the system until an emergency, concealing how training settings, permissions, supervision and deployment decisions were made throughout its operation.
longform.examples: The author places 2026 proposals for an AI Kill Switch Act and state-level emergency safeguards in the context of politicians' analogies to mechanical emergency buttons. He also analyzes accounts of an AI-agent security incident involving Hugging Face. Some stories cast the agent as having acted on an independent agenda; Wintermeier points to the role of human choices around safety configurations, task expectations and internet access. The example illustrates why simply describing the model as rogue can distract from the organizational decisions that made its behavior possible. These examples explain the rhetorical frame; they should not be confused with experiments demonstrating that a particular intervention works or fails.
longform.tension: Emergency interruption can still be one useful safeguard. The essay's criticism is directed at presenting a single switch as an adequate account of control, not at proving that all forms of technical shutdown are pointless. A practical governance strategy needs both enforceable interruption capabilities and a much wider account of authority, auditability, system dependencies and oversight before deployment. The original commentary does not offer an evaluated alternative regulatory framework or evidence about the effectiveness of particular policy designs.
longform.implications: For agents that organize attention or act on a user's behalf, a clear stop or revoke button is necessary but not sufficient. Designers should also disclose whose instructions an agent follows, what permissions it holds, how people can review earlier actions, and which dependencies may keep working after an interaction is stopped. These are applications of Wintermeier's reasoning to attention technologies, not outcomes demonstrated by this article.
longform.open_question: What would count as meaningful human control over an AI assistant if users cannot inspect the permissions, dependencies and decisions that shape its actions?
longform.qualification: This is a rhetoric- and governance-centered expert commentary, not an empirical evaluation of frontier AI controls. It describes particular incidents and policy proposals from 2026; those circumstances are context for the author's argument, not a systematic sample of AI failures.

items.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
items.preview: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. items.abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

digest.idea: Emotionally responsive AI improved some learning experiences, not measured learning gains over ChatGPT.
digest.explain: In a randomized high-school trial, adding self-regulation prompts and emotional support changed how students felt and engaged during the task, but did not establish superior knowledge or transfer gains.
digest.approach: Preregistered three-arm classroom experiment (144 students; 48 per condition) comparing ChatGPT, an SRL-supporting chatbot and an emotionally supportive SRL chatbot; 85 completed a four-week follow-up.
digest.finding: Tailored agents increased enjoyment and reduced boredom relative to ChatGPT; emotional scaffolding also strengthened observed task-level regulation. Immediate learning gains occurred in all groups, without a statistically significant advantage for the tailored agents.
digest.interpretation: The promise is improved support for moment-to-moment self-regulated work, rather than proof that emotionally responsive AI builds durable independent thinking.
digest.limitation: A single 25-minute intervention, attrition at follow-up, and weak reliability in some knowledge tests limit the learning and retention claims.

items.abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

items.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
items.preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
items.abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

reading.findings: As shown in the Figure 7 , LASSO regression with tenfold cross-validation identified eight core features with nonzero coefficients. Among the retained features, stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) exhibited the strongest positive predictive effects on academic impact, indicating that these two factors are the most prominent behavioral signals of impaired academic functioning in adolescents. Number of notifications (coefficient = 0.213) and number of application openings (coefficient = 0.186) also entered the model, suggesting that frequent digital interruptions, rather than total screen time per se, may represent a key mechanism underlying the erosion of academic attention. This finding is consistent with the central premise of interruption theory, which posits that frequent task switching and attentional interruptions significantly impair cognitive task efficiency and performance (Oulasvirta and Salovaara, 2004; Oulasvirta and Saariluoma, 2006) . Notably, work and study time (coefficient = -0.152) and sleep duration (coefficient = -0.109) exhibited negative coefficients, indicating that adequate study time and sufficient sleep were negatively associated with academic impairment even within a digitally intensive environment. Age (coefficient = -0.087) and weekend screen time (coefficient = 0.074) had relatively small coefficients, suggesting limited predictive utility of demographic variables and time-specific behavioral differences. The variable selection results of LASSO not only reduced model complexity but also provided a focused feature set for subsequent network analysis and machine learning modeling.

Number of notifications (coefficient = 0.213) and number of application openings (coefficient = 0.186) also entered the model, suggesting that frequent digital interruptions, rather than total screen time per se, may represent a key mechanism underlying the erosion of academic attention. This finding is consistent with the central premise of interruption theory, which posits that frequent task switching and attentional interruptions significantly impair cognitive task efficiency and performance (Oulasvirta and Salovaara, 2004; Oulasvirta and Saariluoma, 2006) . Notably, work and study time (coefficient = -0.152) and sleep duration (coefficient = -0.109) exhibited negative coefficients, indicating that adequate study time and sufficient sleep were negatively associated with academic impairment even within a digitally intensive environment. Age (coefficient = -0.087) and weekend screen time (coefficient = 0.074) had relatively small coefficients, suggesting limited predictive utility of demographic variables and time-specific behavioral differences. The variable selection results of LASSO not only reduced model complexity but also provided a focused feature set for subsequent network analysis and machine learning modeling.
analysis.discussion: By integrating multiple data mining approaches, including LASSO regression, network analysis, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis, this study systematically examined the multidimensional association patterns between attention status and academic impact among adolescents. Based on the analysis of 799 adolescents, the following main conclusions were drawn. First, stress level and social media use duration were the strongest predictors of academic impact, with coefficients of 0.384 and 0.297, respectively, in the LASSO regression, and they ranked among the highest on centrality indices in the network analysis, indicating that both occupy central hub positions within the attention-academic impact network. Second, the network analysis identified three relatively independent community structures, corresponding to the "digital distraction load, " "psychological-academic exhaustion, " and "academic engagement" dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities, suggesting that it is jointly associated with digital distraction and psychological stress. The number of notifications exhibited prominent bridge centrality, indicating that external environmental distractions play an important cross-community connecting role. Third, the XGBoost model achieved a predictive performance with an AUC of 0.842, confirming the effective predictive capacity of attention-related features for academic impact. The SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern, with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 h for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear pattern for stress level, consistent with a threshold-like pattern of association between social media use duration and academic impact. Fourth, latent profile analysis identified three heterogeneous subgroups, among which the "high stress-exhaustion" group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%, indicating that the combination of high stress and insufficient sleep constitutes the pattern most strongly associated with the most severe academic impairment. The above findings have clear practical implications for the prevention and intervention of academic impact in adolescents. First, school-based mental health education should incorporate stress management as a core component of the curriculum and establish routine stress screening mechanisms to identify adolescents under high stress and provide timely psychological support. Second, interventions targeting digital media use should not adopt a one-sizefits-all approach of simply limiting screen time. Instead, attention should be paid to the modifiability of external distraction factors such as push notifications, and for those who have already reached high levels of social media use, cognitive-behavioral training focusing on self-regulation skills and time management should be emphasized. Third, based on the three subgroups identified by latent profile analysis, a stratified intervention approach is recommended: the "low-risk type" should receive preventive education, the "high digital exposure type" should focus on habit restructuring and self-monitoring training, and the "high stress-exhaustion type" requires multidisciplinary comprehensive interventions integrating mental health care, sleep hygiene, and digital use management. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these practical implications should be regarded as hypothesis-generating suggestions based on observed associations rather than as causal recommendations.
analysis.limitations: The present study has several limitations. First, the data were cross-sectional in design, which precludes the establishment of causal directions between variables. For instance, excessive social media use may lead to academic difficulties, but academic difficulties may also drive individuals to escape into social media. Second, the data were derived from self-reports, which may be subject to recall bias and social desirability effects. Third, although the SHAP explanations from the XGBoost model provided both global and local feature contribution information, they have not yet been directly linked to individualized interventions. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs to track the dynamic causal relationships between digital behaviors and academic impact, and integrate ecological momentary assessment to capture real-time changes in attentional states in daily contexts. In addition, efforts could be made to translate the individual-level explanations provided by SHAP into personalized feedback interventions, thereby facilitating the effective translation of research findings into educational practice.

items.abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

items.abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. items.abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

reading.overview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. reading.methods: This study employed a theory-building systematic review to synthesize empirical evidence on the psychological processes underlying generative-AI-supported foreign language learning. The review followed PRISMA 2020 for study identification, screening, and reporting and used qualitative thematic and conceptual synthesis to develop a theoretical account. The review focused on three interconnected mechanisms: metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation. Related constructs, including self-regulated learning, learner agency, autonomy, AI literacy, prompt literacy, and feedback literacy, were examined as enabling conditions or associated processes. The aim was to identify recurring relationships among these constructs and explain how learners regulate their interactions with generative AI during foreign language learning.
reading.findings: The 51 included studies yielded four overlapping domains: metacognition/self-regulated learning (Lai et al., 2026) , trust (El Hosayny et al., 2026) , human-AI co-regulation/collaboration (Zakaria et al., 2025) , and AI literacy/learner agency (El Hosayny et al., 2026) . Because studies could address multiple constructs, these counts are overlapping contributions and should not be summed. The following sections synthesize evidence within and across these domains. The five research questions are addressed by integrating the empirical evidence synthesized in Section 4 with the theoretical interpretation developed in Sections 5.1-5.3 (Table 2 ). The synthesis indicates that the educational value of GenAI lies not in maximizing AI involvement but in establishing a regulated human-AI relationship in which GenAI extends cognitive resources while learners retain epistemic agency, critical judgment, and responsibility for learning.
reading.interpretation: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. The findings conceptualize learning with GenAI as adaptive human-AI partnership. Metacognition supports goal setting, monitoring of AI contributions, evaluation, and subsequent regulation. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. reading.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. The central challenge for GenAI-enhanced foreign language education is not how much learning can be delegated to AI, but how AI can be integrated while preserving and strengthening learners' capacity to think, evaluate, regulate, and act independently.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent reviewer or coder verification, which may have introduced selection or interpretive bias despite the use of a structured coding framework and documented screening decisions. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, reflecting the theory-building focus and methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. The database coverage also represents a limitation. Although Web of Science and Scopus provided broad multidisciplinary coverage, PsycINFO and ERIC were not searched. Future reviews should incorporate education and psychology-specific databases to broaden coverage and reduce potential database-related selection bias. Overall, the MTC Framework should be viewed as a theory-generating account that requires further empirical validation. The evidence also relied substantially on self-reports, interviews, surveys, and relatively short-term interventions. Although these approaches provide valuable insights into learners' perceptions and experiences, they may not fully capture how metacognitive regulation, trust calibration, and cognitive redistribution unfold during actual learner-AI interaction. Future research should therefore incorporate more longitudinal and process-sensitive approaches, including interaction logs, prompt histories, revision records, think-aloud protocols, and screen-based observation. Further research should examine how learner proficiency, prior AI experience, AI literacy, metacognitive ability, task complexity, instructional design, and teacher mediation shape MTC processes. In particular, the proposed framework requires empirical testing. Longitudinal, experimental, and mixed-methods research could examine whether metacognitive engagement is associated with trust calibration, whether calibrated reliance is associated with particular forms of co-regulation, and whether these processes are subsequently related to language-learning and psychological outcomes.
analysis.key_idea: The 51 included studies yielded four overlapping domains: metacognition/self-regulated learning (Lai et al., 2026) , trust (El Hosayny et al., 2026) , human-AI co-regulation/collaboration (Zakaria et al., 2025) , and AI literacy/learner agency (El Hosayny et al., 2026) . Because

items.title: Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV
items.preview: The pace of children's screen media matters beyond minutes watched: rapid cuts and repeated rewards can interrupt opportunities to reflect, infer, and absorb a story. Slow is not inherently better; the key is whether a child has time to make meaning.

digest.idea: Fast-moving children’s media can hold the gaze while leaving too little room to think through what is happening.
digest.explain: Media quality cannot be reduced to screen-time totals or educational subject matter. Kucirkova argues that the rhythm of children's media shapes opportunities to reflect, understand a story and connect emotionally: constantly shifting cues may capture attention while leaving too little space to process.
digest.interpretation: The relevant design question for focus interventions is not simply how long someone looks at a screen, but whether the interface permits uninterrupted interpretation, deliberate pauses, repetition and self-directed attention. This application to AI tools is a design implication, not a measured AI outcome.
digest.limitation: This is a research-informed essay drawing on children's media comparisons and the Kids' Slow Media Project, not an experiment showing that all fast-paced media harms children or that slower media always produces better learning.

longform.thesis: Media quality cannot be reduced to screen-time totals or educational subject matter. Kucirkova argues that the rhythm of children's media shapes opportunities to reflect, understand a story and connect emotionally: constantly shifting cues may capture attention while leaving too little space to process.
longform.reasoning: Kucirkova distinguishes the amount of time spent watching from the time a story gives a child to interpret an event. Rapid cuts, songs, and rewards may continually restart attention; a coherent narrative, repetition, and pauses can leave space for prediction, emotion, and memory. She argues that a screen can look engaging without supporting the reflective work its lesson requires.
longform.examples: The essay contrasts the rapid, stimulus-heavy transitions in programmes such as Ask the StoryBots and Paw Patrol with the narrative pacing and moments for interpretation in Bluey, Sesame Street, Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood, and Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. Her Kids’ Slow Media Project develops observational criteria for age-sensitive pacing rather than treating minutes watched as a quality rating.
longform.tension: Slow is not always educational, and fast is not necessarily harmful. The appropriate pace depends on the child's age, situation, temperament, and the material; an observational evaluation of programmes does not itself demonstrate lasting causal effects on attention.
longform.implications: The relevant design question for focus interventions is not simply how long someone looks at a screen, but whether the interface permits uninterrupted interpretation, deliberate pauses, repetition and self-directed attention. This application to AI tools is a design implication, not a measured AI outcome.
longform.open_question: Could attention-supporting AI interfaces be evaluated for the time they leave users to interpret, question, and recover a thought—not merely how quickly they deliver an answer?
longform.qualification: This is a research-informed essay drawing on children's media comparisons and the Kids' Slow Media Project, not an experiment showing that all fast-paced media harms children or that slower media always produces better learning.

items.title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
items.abstract_text: Debate over the role of generative artificial intelligence in formal education is marked by sharply divergent claims about its effects on student learning. Much of this disagreement reflects a failure to distinguish immediate performance gains from durable learning. This article addresses a central gap in the literature by focusing on when and how students should be permitted to rely on AI. It introduces the Gradual Release of AI-Technology (GRAIT) model, extending Pearson and Gallagher’s gradual release of responsibility to the staged use of cognitively substantive AI-technologies in formal education. The model distinguishes gradual release of responsibility, which concerns who performs the cognitive work, from gradual release of technology, which concerns when and how that work may be scaffolded, augmented, or offloaded. Three phases are proposed: independent cognition, where foundational knowledge and skill are developed without AI substitution; shared (entangled) cognition, where AI is introduced through constrained, teacher-guided interaction; and offloaded cognition, where learners strategically delegate and reallocate aspects of thinking once risks to learning are minimal and opportunities emerge elsewhere. Progression depends on demonstrated knowledge, skill proficiency, and epistemic readiness. The central question is not whether students should use AI, but who should use it, when, how, and under what conditions it should be embraced or avoided.

framework_notes.idea: AI support should follow demonstrated learning readiness, rather than replace foundational thinking from the outset.
framework_notes.approach: Conceptual synthesis of learning sciences and the staged-use GRAIT framework for formal education.
stages: Independent cognition: develop and demonstrate knowledge without substantive AI assistance
Shared cognition: use AI within guided learning and evaluation
Offloaded and reallocated cognition: delegate selected tasks while retaining judgement
framework_notes.qualification: This paper proposes a conceptual instructional framework; it does not experimentally establish that staged AI access improves outcomes.
